Epic Games has filed its response to Apple's request for the court to order settlement talks, in the long-running App Store lawsuit. Here are the details.

Epic believes court-mandated settlement talks would be of no benefit

Last Thursday, Apple filed its proposed commission structure for in-app purchases made outside of its App Store system in the United States.

Under Apple's proposed structure, Apple would charge a maximum 15% commission on purchases completed through alternative payment systems.

On the same day, Apple filed a separate motion requesting Judge Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

Apple stated in its motion that "discussing potential settlement solutions in a confidential, non-adversarial environment will increase the chances of reaching a pragmatic resolution, thereby avoiding a lengthy remand procedure."

Epic has now responded to Apple's motion, stating that although the company "has always been, and remains, willing to accept any sincere settlement proposal put forward by Apple to introduce competition and benefit all developers," it "does not believe that a referral to a settlement conference at this stage can materially advance the prospects of such a settlement."

Epic added in its response that "if the court orders a referral to a settlement conference, Epic will participate in good faith."

It now falls to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to determine whether to refer the case to a settlement conference. Apple has requested that the conference be conducted under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.

9to5Mac's take

Apple has repeatedly attempted to narrow the scope of the injunction issued by Judge Gonzalez Rogers regarding purchases outside the App Store. Apple has particularly argued that, since Epic's lawsuit is not a class action, the injunction should not broadly apply to other developers.

For instance, in one of its appeals, Apple argued that developers seeking similar relief should file their own lawsuits rather than benefit from the injunction in Epic's case. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Apple's attempt to narrow the injunction's scope, ruling that limiting it to Epic and its affiliates would fail to provide Epic with the complete relief it seeks.

This ruling is also consistent with Epic's publicly stated position throughout most of the case — that its fight goes beyond its own commercial interests and aims to benefit the broader developer community.

In its motion requesting the case be referred to (confidential) settlement talks, Apple did not indicate what conditions it might propose. However, anyone closely following this case would likely agree that Apple is probably seeking a deal particularly attractive to Epic, while limiting any concessions to Epic itself.

In fact, Epic's response has preemptively shut down this idea, stating that Apple's "sincere settlement proposal" must "benefit all developers," and hinting at the end of its response that Apple's efforts may be too little, too late.

If you were Apple, what conditions would you offer Epic Games? Let us know in the comments.
